changelog: Insert a concise core principle requiring cuts to keep short (1–4 word) complements with their predicate — addresses the primary finding that such short continuations are essential.
Delete Example E7 (largest) to free prompt budget; kept remaining examples to preserve varied cases.
Delete Example E4 (second-largest) to meet size constraints while removing less-essential, lengthy examples.
Delete Example E8 (third-largest) to recover sufficient characters for the new principle.
findings: The prompt under-detects short complements that actually complete the preceding predicate: it treats cuts before brief measures, temporal/locative phrases, directional words, or negating/infinitival complements as safe when they are essential to the clause's truth.

diagnosis.why: Inserting the new principle made the model prefer keeping very short (1–4 word) complements attached to their predicate, so cuts moved later and improved cohesion mainly for longer pieces and lists (largest gains in the ≤99/≤10/≤7 bins), but that same shift caused more harmful splits in short/medium contexts (some ≤3–≤7 pairs got worse). Removing Examples E7/E4/E8 removed counterexamples that would have constrained those bad short-context moves.
diagnosis.lesson: A later revision should respect that preserving 1–4-word predicate complements improves long-span cohesion but must keep examples (or guidance) that prevent creating subject–verb or other harmful short-context splits.
blamed: Insert concise core principle (keep short 1–4 word complements with predicate)

changelog: delete C3 — Remove the short-complement binding that pushed cuts after subjects and away from verbs. History blamed C3 for harming very-short latency bins and producing subject–verb splits; deleting it reduces that harmful bias and avoids restating what C2/C6 already cover.
findings: The prompt undervalues keeping a short subject attached to its verb: it lets cuts isolate the verb (or verb phrase) from a immediately preceding short subject, producing orphaned predicates or apparent contradictions.

edits.was: - Do the next one to four words form a short complement that completes the immed

diagnosis.why: Removing C3 eliminated the short-complement binding that had discouraged cuts near verbs, so the model began placing more cuts earlier/around predicates; that produced modest gains for longer-latency pieces (by_bin shows the biggest positive change in the ≤99 and mid-length bins) but also increased harmful subject–verb splits and fragmented enumerations in short/medium bins, leaving the overall H_set change near zero.
diagnosis.lesson: If you remove the short-complement binding, you must preserve a constraint that prevents cutting immediately between subjects and their verbs and that avoids splitting list items, because deletion alone trades away those short-bin harms for only modest long-bin gains.
